entries.99440725f21e64d05c4e63ab03342857a3c805c6: <div sID="gen8930" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="13" osisID="Neh.13" sID="Neh.13"/> <div eID="gen8930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8931" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8932" type="x-p"/> Nehemiah, having finished what he undertook for the fencing and filling of the holy city, returned to the king his master, who was not willing to be long without him, as appears (<reference osisRef="Neh.13.6">v. 6</reference>). But, after some time, he obtained leave to come back again to Jerusalem, to redress grievances, and purge out some corruptions which had crept in in his absence; and very active he was in reforming several abuses, which here we have an account of. I. He turned out from Israel the mixed multitude, the Moabites and Ammonites especially, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.1-Neh.13.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. With a particular indignation, he expelled Tobiah out of the lodgings he had got in the court of the temple, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.4-Neh.13.9">ver. 4-9</reference>. II. He secured the maintenance of the priests and Levites to them more firmly than it had been, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.10-Neh.13.14">ver. 10-14</reference>. III. He restrained the profanation of the sabbath day, and provided for the due sanctification of it, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.15-Neh.13.22">ver. 15-22</reference>. IV. He checked the growing mischief of marrying strange wives, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.23-Neh.13.31">ver. 23-31</reference>.
entries.f7a4962eaa214b4d772d1857b0f5d67afa94463e: <div eID="gen8932" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8931" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The People's Attention to Their Duty. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 444.)</title> <div sID="gen8933" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> On that day they read in the book of Moses in the audience of the people; and therein was found written, that the Ammonite and the Moabite should not come into the congregation of God for ever; <hi type="super">2</hi> Because they met not the children of Israel with bread and with water, but hired Balaam against them, that he should curse them: howbeit our God turned the curse into a blessing. <hi type="super">3</hi> Now it came to pass, when they had heard the law, that they separated from Israel all the mixed multitude. <hi type="super">4</hi> And before this, Eliashib the priest, having the oversight of the chamber of the house of our God, <hi type="italic">was</hi> allied unto Tobiah: <hi type="super">5</hi> And he had prepared for him a great chamber, where aforetime they laid the meat offerings, the frankincense, and the vessels, and the tithes of the corn, the new wine, and the oil, which was commanded <hi type="italic">to be given</hi> to the Levites, and the singers, and the porters; and the offerings of the priests. <hi type="super">6</hi> But in all this <hi type="italic">time</hi> was not I at Jerusalem: for in the two and thirtieth year of Artaxerxes king of Babylon came I unto the king, and after certain days obtained I leave of the king: <hi type="super">7</hi> And I came to Jerusalem, and understood of the evil that Eliashib did for Tobiah, in preparing him a chamber in the courts of the house of God. <hi type="super">8</hi> And it grieved me sore: therefore I cast forth all the household stuff of Tobiah out of the chamber. <hi type="super">9</hi> Then I commanded, and they cleansed the chambers: and thither brought I again the vessels of the house of God, with the meat offering and the frankincense. <div eID="gen8933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8934" type="x-p"/> It was the honour of Israel, and the greatest preservation of their holiness, that they were a peculiar people, and were so to keep themselves, and not to mingle with the nations, nor suffer any of them to incorporate with them. Now here we have, <div eID="gen8934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8935" type="x-p"/> I. The law to this purport, which happened to be read <hi type="italic">on that day, in the audience of the people</hi> (<reference osisRef="Neh.13.1">v. 1</reference>), on the day of the dedication of the wall, as it should seem, for with their prayers and praises they joined the reading of the word; and though it was long after that the other grievances, here mentioned, were redressed by Nehemiah's power, yet this of the mixed multitude might be redressed then by the people's own act, for so it seems to be, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.3">v. 3</reference>. Or, perhaps, it was on the anniversary commemoration of that day, some years after, and therefore said to be <hi type="italic">on that day.</hi> They found a law, that the Ammonites and Moabites should not be naturalized, should not settle among them, nor unite with them, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.1">v. 1</reference>. The reason given is because they had been injurious and ill-natured to the Israel of God (<reference osisRef="Neh.13.2">v. 2</reference>), had not shown them common civility, but sought their ruin, though they not only did them no harm, but were expressly forbidden to do them any. This law we have, with this reason, <reference osisRef="Deut.23.3-Deut.23.5">Deut. xxiii. 3-5</reference>. <div eID="gen8935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8936" type="x-p"/> II. The people's ready compliance with this law, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.3">v. 3</reference>. See the benefit of the public reading of the word of God; when it is duly attended to it discovers to us sin and duty, good and evil, and shows us wherein we have erred. Then we profit by the discovery when by it we are wrought upon to separate ourselves from all that evil to which we had addicted ourselves. They <hi type="italic">separated from Israel all the mixed multitude,</hi> which had of old been a snare to them, for the <hi type="italic">mixed multitude fell a lusting,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.11.4">Num. xi. 4</reference>. These inmates they expelled, as usurpers and dangerous. <div eID="gen8936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8937" type="x-p"/> III. The particular case of Tobiah, who was an Ammonite, and to whom, it is likely, the historian had an eye in the recital of the law (<reference osisRef="Neh.13.1">v. 1</reference>), and the reason of it, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.2">v. 2</reference>. For he had the same enmity to Israel that his ancestors had, the spirit of an Ammonite, witness his indignation at Nehemiah (<reference osisRef="Neh.2.10">ch. ii. 10</reference>) and the opposition he had given to his undertakings, <reference osisRef="Neh.4.7-Neh.4.8">ch. iv. 7, 8</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen8937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8938" type="x-p"/> 1. How basely Eliashib the chief priest took this Tobiah in to be a lodger even in the courts of the temple. (1.) He was allied to Tobiah (<reference osisRef="Neh.13.4">v. 4</reference>), by marriage first and then by friendship. His grandson had married Sanballat's daughter, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.28">v. 28</reference>. Probably some other of his family had married Tobiah's, and (would you think it?) the high priest thought the alliance an honour to his family, and was very proud of it, though really it was his greatest disgrace, and what he had reason to be ashamed of. It was expressly provided by the law that the high priest should marry <hi type="italic">one of his own people,</hi> else he <hi type="italic">profanes his seed among his people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.21.14-Lev.21.15">Lev. xxi. 14, 15</reference>. And for Eliashib to contract an alliance with an Ammonite, a <hi type="italic">servant</hi> (for so he is called) and to value himself upon it, probably because he has a wit and a beau, and cried up for a fine gentleman (<reference osisRef="Neh.6.19">ch. vi. 19</reference>), was such a contempt of the crown of his consecration as one would not wish should be told in Gath or published in the streets of Ashkelon. (2.) Being allied to him, he must be acquainted with him. Tobiah, being a man of business, has often occasion to be at Jerusalem, I doubt upon no good design. Eliashib is fond of his new kinsman, pleased with his company, and must have him as near him as he can. He has not a room for him stately enough in his own apartment, in the courts of the temple; therefore, out of several little chambers which had been used for store-chambers, by taking down the partitions, he contrived to make one great chamber, a state-room for Tobiah, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.5">v. 5</reference>. A wretched thing it was, [1.] That Tobiah the Ammonite should be entertained with respect in Israel, and have a magnificent reception. [2.] That the high priest, who should have taught the people the law and set them a good example, should, contrary to the law, give him entertainment, and make use of the power he had, as overseer of the chambers of the temple, for that purpose. [3.] That he should lodge him in the courts of God's house, as if to confront God himself; this was next to setting up an idol there, as the wicked kings of old had done. An Ammonite must not <hi type="italic">come into the congregation;</hi> and shall one of the worst and vilest of the Ammonites be courted into the temple itself, and caressed there? [4.] That he should throw out the stores of the temple, to make room for him, and so expose them to be lost, wasted, and embezzled, though they were the <hi type="italic">portions of the priests,</hi> merely to gratify Tobiah. Thus did he <hi type="italic">corrupt the covenant of Levi,</hi> as Malachi complained at this time, <reference osisRef="Neh.2.8">ch. ii. 8</reference>. Well might Nehemiah add (<reference osisRef="Neh.13.6">v. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">But all this time was not I at Jerusalem.</hi> If he had been there, the high priest durst not have done such a thing. The envious one, who sows tares in God's field, knows how to take an opportunity to do it when the <hi type="italic">servants sleep</hi> or are absent, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.25">Matt. xiii. 25</reference>. The golden calf was made when Moses was in the mount. <div eID="gen8938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8939" type="x-p"/> 2. How bravely Nehemiah, the chief governor, threw him out, and all that belonged to him, and restored the chambers to their proper use. When he came to Jerusalem, and was informed by the good people who were troubled at it what an intimacy had grown between their chief priest and their chief enemy, it <hi type="italic">grieved him sorely</hi> (<reference osisRef="Neh.13.7-Neh.13.8">v. 7, 8</reference>) that God's house should be so profaned, his enemies so caressed and trusted, and his cause betrayed by him that should have been its protector and patron. Nothing grieves a good man, a good magistrate, more than to see the ministers of God's house do any wicked thing. Nehemiah has power and he will use it for God. (1.) Tobiah shall be expelled. He fears not disobliging him, fears not his resentments, or Eliashib's, nor excuses himself from interposing in an affair that lay within the jurisdiction of the high priest; but, like one zealously affected in a good thing, he expels the intruder, by casting forth all his household stuff. He did not seize it for his own use, but cast it out, that Tobiah, who it is probable was now absent, when he came again, might have no conveniences for his reception there. Our Saviour thus <hi type="italic">cleansed the temple,</hi> that the <hi type="italic">house of prayer</hi> might not be a <hi type="italic">den of thieves.</hi> And thus those that would expel sin out of their hearts, those living temples, must throw out its household stuff and all the provision made for it, strip it, starve it, and take away all those things that are the food and fuel of lust; this is, in effect, to mortify it. (2.) The temple stores shall be brought in again, and the <hi type="italic">vessels of the house of God put in their places;</hi> but the chambers must first be sprinkled with the water of purification, and so cleansed, because they had been profaned. Thus, when sin is cast out of the heart by repentance, let the blood of Christ be applied to it by faith, and then let it be furnished with the graces of God's Spirit for every good work.
entries.8491b25fda802149b9a0cbeb63b6420f8853703f: <div eID="gen8939" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Abuses Rectified. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 434.)</title> <div sID="gen8940" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> And I perceived that the portions of the Levites had not been given <hi type="italic">them:</hi> for the Levites and the singers, that did the work, were fled every one to his field. <hi type="super">11</hi> Then contended I with the rulers, and said, Why is the house of God forsaken? And I gathered them together, and set them in their place. <hi type="super">12</hi> Then brought all Judah the tithe of the corn and the new wine and the oil unto the treasuries. <hi type="super">13</hi> And I made treasurers over the treasuries, Shelemiah the priest, and Zadok the scribe, and of the Levites, Pedaiah: and next to them <hi type="italic">was</hi> Hanan the son of Zaccur, the son of Mattaniah: for they were counted faithful, and their office <hi type="italic">was</hi> to distribute unto their brethren. <hi type="super">14</hi> Remember me, O my God, concerning this, and wipe not out my good deeds that I have done for the house of my God, and for the offices thereof. <div eID="gen8940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8941" type="x-p"/> Here is another grievance redressed by Nehemiah. <div eID="gen8941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8942" type="x-p"/> I. The Levites had been wronged. This was the grievance: their <hi type="italic">portions had not been given them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Neh.13.10">v. 10</reference>. Perhaps Tobiah, when he took possession of the store-chambers, seized the stores too, and, by the connivance of Eliashib, converted them to his own use. The complaint is not that they were not collected from the people, but that they were not given to the Levites, and the Levites were so modest as not to sue for them; <hi type="italic">for the Levites and singers fled every one to his field.</hi> This comes in as a reason either, (1.) Why their payments were withheld. The Levites were non-residents: when they should have been doing their work about the temple, they were at their farms in the country; and therefore the people were little inclined to give them their maintenance. If ministers have not the encouragement they should have, let them consider whether they themselves be not accessory to the contempt they are under, by the neglect of their business. Or rather, (2.) It is the reason why Nehemiah soon perceived that their dues had been denied them, because he missed them from their posts. "Where are the singers" (said Nehemiah); "why do not they attend according to their office, to praise God?" "Why, truly, they have gone every one to his country seat, to get a livelihood for themselves and their families out of their grounds; for their profession would not maintain them." A scandalous maintenance makes a scandalous ministry. The work is neglected because the workmen are. It was not long since the payment of the salaries appointed for the singers was put into a very good method (<reference osisRef="Neh.12.47">ch. xii. 47</reference>); and yet how soon did it fail for want of being looked after! <div eID="gen8942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8943" type="x-p"/> II. Nehemiah laid the fault upon the rulers, who should have taken care that the Levites minded their business and had all due encouragement therein. This is required from Christian magistrates, that they use their power to oblige ministers to do their duty, and people to do theirs. Nehemiah began with the rulers, and called them to an account: "<hi type="italic">Why is the house of God forsaken?</hi> <reference osisRef="Neh.13.11">v. 11</reference>. Why are the Levites starved out of it? Why did not you take notice of this and prevent it?" The people <hi type="italic">forsook the Levites,</hi> which was expressly forbidden (<reference osisRef="Deut.12.19">Deut. xii. 19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.14.27">xiv. 27</reference>); and then the Levites forsook their post in the house of God. Both ministers and people who forsake religion and the services of it, and magistrates too who do not what they can to keep them to it, will have a great deal to answer for. <div eID="gen8943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8944" type="x-p"/> III. He delayed not to bring the dispersed Levites to <hi type="italic">their places</hi> again, and set them in <hi type="italic">their stations</hi> (as the word is), <reference osisRef="Neh.13.11">v. 11</reference>. A Levite in his field (<hi type="italic">clericus in foro—a minister keeping the market</hi>) is out of his station. God's house is his place, and there let him be found. Many that are careless would do much better than they do if they were but called upon. <hi type="italic">Say to Archippus, Take heed to thy ministry.</hi> <div eID="gen8944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8945" type="x-p"/> IV. He obliged the people to bring in their tithes, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.12">v. 12</reference>. His zeal provoked theirs; and, when they saw the Levites at their work, they could not for shame withhold their wages any longer, but honestly and cheerfully brought them in. The better church-work is done the better will church-dues be paid. <div eID="gen8945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8946" type="x-p"/> V. He provided that just and prompt payment should be made of the Levites' stipends. Commissioners were appointed to see to this (<reference osisRef="Neh.13.13">v. 13</reference>), and they were such as <hi type="italic">were accounted faithful,</hi> that is, had approved themselves so in other trusts committed to them, and so had <hi type="italic">purchased to themselves this good degree,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.13">1 Tim. iii. 13</reference>. Let men be tried first and then trusted, tried in the less and then trusted with more. Their office was to receive and pay, to distribute to their brethren in due season and due proportions. <div eID="gen8946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8947" type="x-p"/> VI. Having no recompence (it is a question whether he had thanks) from those for whom he did these good services, he looks up to God as his paymaster (<reference osisRef="Neh.13.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">Remember me, O my God! concerning this.</hi> Nehemiah was a man much in pious ejaculations; on every occasion he looked up to God, and committed himself and his affairs to him. 1. He here reflects with comfort and much satisfaction upon what he had done for the house of God and the offices thereof; it pleased him to think that he had been any way instrumental to revive and support religion in his country and to reform what was amiss. What kindness any show to God's ministers, thus shall it be returned into their own bosoms, in the secret joy they shall have there, not only in having done well, but in having done good, good to many, good to souls. 2. He here refers it to God to consider him for it, not in pride, or as boasting of what he had done, much less depending upon it as his righteousness, or as if he thought he had made God a debtor to him, but in a humble appeal to him concerning his integrity and honest intention in what he had done, and a believing expectation that he would not be unrighteous to <hi type="italic">forget his work and labour of love,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.6.10">Heb. vi. 10</reference>. Observe how modest he is in his requests. He only prays, <hi type="italic">Remember me,</hi> not <hi type="italic">Reward me—Wipe not out my good deeds,</hi> not <hi type="italic">Publish them, Record them.</hi> Yet he was rewarded and his good deeds were recorded; for God does more than we are able to ask. Note, Deeds done <hi type="italic">for the house of God and the offices of it,</hi> for the support of religion and the encouragement of it, are good deeds. There is both righteousness and godliness in them, and God will certainly remember them, and not wipe them out; they shall in no wise lose their reward.
entries.381cee7653850ae72b1b745cbd1c9b9d2aa0e374: <div eID="gen8947" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Charge Respecting the Sabbath. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 434.)</title> <div sID="gen8948" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> In those days saw I in Judah <hi type="italic">some</hi> treading wine presses on the sabbath, and bringing in sheaves, and lading asses; as also wine, grapes, and figs, and all <hi type="italic">manner of</hi> burdens, which they brought into Jerusalem on the sabbath day: and I testified <hi type="italic">against them</hi> in the day wherein they sold victuals. <hi type="super">16</hi> There dwelt men of Tyre also therein, which brought fish, and all manner of ware, and sold on the sabbath unto the children of Judah, and in Jerusalem. <hi type="super">17</hi> Then I contended with the nobles of Judah, and said unto them, What evil thing <hi type="italic">is</hi> this that ye do, and profane the sabbath day? <hi type="super">18</hi> Did not your fathers thus, and did not our God bring all this evil upon us, and upon this city? yet ye bring more wrath upon Israel by profaning the sabbath. <hi type="super">19</hi> And it came to pass, that when the gates of Jerusalem began to be dark before the sabbath, I commanded that the gates should be shut, and charged that they should not be opened till after the sabbath: and <hi type="italic">some</hi> of my servants set I at the gates, <hi type="italic">that</hi> there should no burden be brought in on the sabbath day. <hi type="super">20</hi> So the merchants and sellers of all kind of ware lodged without Jerusalem once or twice. <hi type="super">21</hi> Then I testified against them, and said unto them, Why lodge ye about the wall? if ye do <hi type="italic">so</hi> again, I will lay hands on you. From that time forth came they no <hi type="italic">more</hi> on the sabbath. <hi type="super">22</hi> And I commanded the Levites that they should cleanse themselves, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> they should come <hi type="italic">and</hi> keep the gates, to sanctify the sabbath day. Remember me, O my God, <hi type="italic">concerning</hi> this also, and spare me according to the greatness of thy mercy. <div eID="gen8948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8949" type="x-p"/> Here is another instance of that blessed reformation in which Nehemiah was so active. He revived sabbath-sanctification, and maintained the authority of the fourth commandment; and a very good deed this was for the house of God and the offices thereof, for, where holy time is over-looked and made nothing of, it is not strange if all holy duties be neglected. Here is, <div eID="gen8949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8950" type="x-p"/> I. A remonstrance of the abuse. The law of the sabbath was very strict and much insisted one, and with good reason, for religion is never in the throne while sabbaths are trodden under foot. But Nehemiah discovered even in Judah, among those to whom sabbaths were given for a sign, this law wretchedly violated. His own eyes were his informers. Magistrates who are in care to discharge their duty aright will as much as may be <hi type="italic">see with their own eyes,</hi> and <hi type="italic">accomplish a diligent search</hi> to find out that which is evil. To his great grief it appeared that there was a general profanation of the sabbath, that holy day, even in Jerusalem, that holy city, which was so lately dedicated to God. 1. The husbandmen trod their wine-presses and brought home their corn on that day (<reference osisRef="Neh.13.15">v. 15</reference>), through there was an express command that <hi type="italic">in earing-time, and in harvest-time, they should rest</hi> on the sabbaths (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.21">Exod. xxxiv. 21</reference>), because then they might be tempted to take a greater liberty, and to fancy that God would indulge them in it. 2. The carriers <hi type="italic">loaded their asses with all manner of burdens,</hi> and made no scruple of it, though there was a particular proviso in the law for the cattle resting (<reference osisRef="Deut.5.14">Deut. v. 14</reference>) and that they should <hi type="italic">bear no burden on the sabbath day,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.17.21">Jer. xvii. 21</reference>. 3. The hawkers, and pedlars, and petty chapmen, that were men of Tyre, that famous trading city, <hi type="italic">sold all manner of wares</hi> on the sabbath day (<reference osisRef="Neh.13.16">v. 16</reference>); and the children of Judah and Jerusalem had so little grace as to buy of them, and so encourage them in making our Father's day a day of merchandise, contrary to the law of the fourth commandment, which forbids the <hi type="italic">doing any manner of work.</hi> No wonder there was a general decay of religion and corruption of manners among this people when they <hi type="italic">forsook the sanctuary</hi> and <hi type="italic">profaned the sabbath.</hi> <div eID="gen8950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8951" type="x-p"/> II. The reformation of it. Those that are jealous for the honour of God cannot bear to see his sabbath profaned. Observe in what method this good man proceeded in his zeal for the sabbath. <div eID="gen8951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8952" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">He testified against those</hi> who profaned it, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.15">v. 15</reference>, and again <reference osisRef="Neh.13.21">v. 21</reference>. He not only expressed his own dislike of it, but endeavoured to convince them that it was a great sin, and showed them the testimony of the word of God against it. He would not punish it till he had laid open the evil of it. <div eID="gen8952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8953" type="x-p"/> 2. He reasoned with the rulers concerning it, took the nobles of Judah to task, and contended with them, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.17">v. 17</reference>. The greatest of men are not too high to be told of their faults by those whose proper office it is to reprove them; nay, great men should be, as here, contended with in the first place, because of the influence they have upon others. <div eID="gen8953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8954" type="x-p"/> (1.) He charges them with it: <hi type="italic">You do it.</hi> They did not carry corn, nor sell fish, but, [1.] They connived at those that did, and did not use their power to restrain them, and so made themselves guilty, as those magistrates do who bear the sword in vain. [2.] They set a bad example in other things. If the nobles allowed themselves in sports and recreations, in idle visits and idle talk, on the sabbath day, the men of business, both in city and country, would profane it by their worldly employments, as more justifiable. We must be responsible for the sins which others are led to commit by our example. <div eID="gen8954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8955" type="x-p"/> (2.) He charges it upon them as an evil thing, for so it is, proceeding from a great contempt of God and our own souls. <div eID="gen8955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8956" type="x-p"/> (3.) He reasons the case with them (<reference osisRef="Neh.13.18">v. 18</reference>), and shows them that sabbath breaking was one of the sins for which God had brought judgments upon them, and that if they did not take warning, but returned to the same sins again, they had reason to expect further judgments: <hi type="italic">You bring more wrath upon Israel by profaning the sabbath.</hi> Thus Ezra concluded, <hi type="italic">If we again break thy commandments, wilt not thou be angry with us till thou hast consumed us?</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezra.9.14">Ezra ix. 14</reference>. <div eID="gen8956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8957" type="x-p"/> 3. He took care to prevent the profanation of the sabbath, as one that aimed only at reformation. If he could reform them, he would not punish them, and, if he should punish them, it was but that he might reform them. This is an example to magistrates to be heirs of restraint, and prudently to use the bit and bridle, that there may be no occasion for the lash. (1.) He ordered the gates of Jerusalem to be kept shut from the evening before the sabbath to the morning after, and set his own servants (whose care, courage and honesty, he could confide in) to watch them, that no burdens should be brought in on the sabbath day, nor late the night before, nor early in the morning after, lest sabbath time should be encroached upon, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.19">v. 19</reference>. Those that came in to worship in the courts of the temple were no doubt admitted to pass and repass, but none that came to sell goods; <hi type="italic">they</hi> were forced to <hi type="italic">lodge without the city</hi> (<reference osisRef="Neh.13.20">v. 20</reference>), where no doubt they wished the sabbath were gone, that they might sell corn. (2.) He threatened those who came with goods to the gates, who pressed hard for entrance, telling them that, if they came again, he would certainly lay hands on them (<reference osisRef="Neh.13.21">v. 21</reference>), and this deterred them from coming any more. Note, If reformers will but put on resolution, more may be done towards the breaking of bad customs than they can imagine. Vice connived at is indeed a daring thing, and will bid defiance to counsel and reproof; but it may be made cowardly, and will be so when magistrates make themselves a terror to it. <hi type="italic">The king that sits on the throne of judgment scatters away all evil with his eyes.</hi> (3.) He charged the Levites to take care about the due sanctifying of the sabbath, that they should cleanse themselves in the first place, and so give a good example to the people, and <hi type="italic">that they should</hi> some of them <hi type="italic">come and keep the gates,</hi> <reference osisRef="Neh.13.22">v. 22</reference>. Because he and his servants must shortly return to court, he would leave this charge with some that might abide by it, that not only when he was present, but in his absence, the sabbath might be sanctified. Then there is likely to be a reformation, in this and other respects, when magistrates and ministers join their forces. The courage, zeal, and prudence of Nehemiah in this matter, are here recorded for our imitation; and we have reason to think that the cure he wrought was lasting; for, in our Saviour's time, we find the Jews in the other extreme, over-scrupulous in the ceremonial part of sabbath-sanctification. <div eID="gen8957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8958" type="x-p"/> 4. He concludes this passage with a prayer (<reference osisRef="Neh.13.22">v. 22</reference>), in which observe, (1.) The petitions: <hi type="italic">Remember me</hi> (as the thief on the cross, <hi type="italic">Lord, remember me</hi>); that is enough. God's thoughts to us ward are very precious, <reference osisRef="Ps.40.5">Ps. xl. 5</reference>. He adds, <hi type="italic">Spare me.</hi> So far is he from thinking that what he had done did properly merit a reward in strict justice that he cries earnestly to God to <hi type="italic">spare him,</hi> as Jeremiah (<reference osisRef="Neh.15.15">ch. xv. 15</reference>), <hi type="italic">Take me not away in thy long-suffering</hi> (<reference osisRef="Neh.10.24">ch. x. 24</reference>), <hi type="italic">Correct me not in anger,</hi> and (<reference osisRef="Neh.17.17">ch. xvii. 17</reference>), <hi type="italic">Be not a terror to me.</hi> Note, The best saints, even when they do the best actions, stand in need of <hi type="italic">sparing mercy;</hi> for <hi type="italic">there is not a just man that doeth good and sinneth not.</hi> (2.) The plea: <hi type="italic">According to the greatness</hi> (or multitude) <hi type="italic">of thy mercies.</hi> Note, God's mercy is what we must depend upon, and not any merit of our own, when we appear before God.
entries.5e7493d4e9271350b50bc2c767e227cd94188d6a: <div eID="gen8958" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Dismissal of Strange Wives. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 434.)</title> <div sID="gen8959" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> In those days also saw I Jews <hi type="italic">that</hi> had married wives of Ashdod, of Ammon, <hi type="italic">and</hi> of Moab: <hi type="super">24</hi> And their children spake half in the speech of Ashdod, and could not speak in the Jews' language, but according to the language of each people. <hi type="super">25</hi> And I contended with them, and cursed them, and smote certain of them, and plucked off their hair, and made them swear by God, <hi type="italic">saying,</hi> Ye shall not give your daughters unto their sons, nor take their daughters unto your sons, or for yourselves. <hi type="super">26</hi> Did not Solomon king of Israel sin by these things? yet among many nations was there no king like him, who was beloved of his God, and God made him king over all Israel: nevertheless even him did outlandish women cause to sin. <hi type="super">27</hi> Shall we then hearken unto you to do all this great evil, to transgress against our God in marrying strange wives? <hi type="super">28</hi> And <hi type="italic">one</hi> of the sons of Joiada, the son of Eliashib the high priest, <hi type="italic">was</hi> son in law to Sanballat the Horonite: therefore I chased him from me. <hi type="super">29</hi> Remember them, O my God, because they have defiled the priesthood, and the covenant of the priesthood, and of the Levites. <hi type="super">30</hi> Thus cleansed I them from all strangers, and appointed the wards of the priests and the Levites, every one in his business; <hi type="super">31</hi> And for the wood offering, at times appointed, and for the firstfruits. Remember me, O my God, for good. <div eID="gen8959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8960" type="x-p"/> We have here one instance more of Nehemiah's pious zeal for the purifying of his countrymen as a peculiar people to God; that was the thing he aimed at in the use of his power, not the enriching of himself. See here, <div eID="gen8960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8961" type="x-p"/> I. How they had corrupted themselves by marrying strange wives. This was complained of in Ezra's time, and much done towards a reformation, <reference osisRef="Ezra.9.1-Ezra.10.44">Ezra ix. and x.</reference> But, when the unclean spirit is cast out, if a watchful eye be not kept upon him, he will re-enter; so he did here. Though in Ezra's time those that had married strange wives were forced to put them away, which could not but occasion trouble and confusion in families, yet others would not take warning. <hi type="italic">Nitimur in vetitum—we still lean towards what is forbidden.</hi> Nehemiah, like a good governor, enquired into the state of the families of those that were under his charge, that he might reform what was amiss in them, and so heal the streams by healing the springs. 1. He enquired whence they had their wives, and found that many of the Jews had <hi type="italic">married wives of Ashdod, of Ammon, and of Moab</hi> (<reference osisRef="Neh.13.23">v. 23</reference>), either because they were fond of what was far-fetched or because they hoped by these alliances to strengthen and enrich themselves. See how God by the prophet reproves this, <reference osisRef="Mal.2.11">Mal. ii. 11</reference>. <hi type="italic">Judah has dealt treacherously,</hi> and broken covenant with God, the covenant made in Ezra's time with reference to this very thing; he has <hi type="italic">profaned the holiness of the Lord</hi> by <hi type="italic">marrying the daughter</hi> (that is, the worshipper) <hi type="italic">of a strange god.</hi> 2. He talked with the children, and found they were <hi type="italic">children of strangers,</hi> for their <hi type="italic">speech betrayed them.</hi> The children were bred up with their mothers, and learned of them and their nurses and servants to speak, so that they could not speak the Jews' language, could not speak it at all, or not readily, or not purely, but <hi type="italic">half in the speech of Ashdod,</hi> or Ammon, or Moab, according as the country was which the mother was a native of. Observe, (1.) Children, in their childhood, learn much of their mothers. <hi type="italic">Partus sequitur ventrem—they are prone to imitate their mothers.</hi> (2.) If either side be bad, the corrupt nature will incline the children to take after that, which is a good reason why Christians should not be unequally yoked. (3.) In the education of children great care should be taken about the government of their tongues, that they learn not the language of Ashdod, any impious or impure talk, any corrupt communication. <div eID="gen8961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8962" type="x-p"/> II. What course Nehemiah took to purge out this corruption, when he discovered how much it had prevailed. <div eID="gen8962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8963" type="x-p"/> 1. He showed them the evil of it, and the obligation he lay under to witness against it. He did not seek an occasion against them, but this was an iniquity to be punished by the judge, and which he must by no means connive at (<reference osisRef="Neh.13.27">v. 27</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Shall we hearken to you,</hi> who endeavour to palliate and excuse it? No, it is an evil, a great evil, it is a <hi type="italic">transgression against our God, to marry strange wives,</hi> and we must do our utmost to put a stop to it. You beg that they may not be divorced from you, but we cannot hearken to you, for there is no other remedy to clear us from the guilt and prevent infection." (1.) He quotes a precept, to prove that it was in itself a great sin; and makes them swear to that precept: <hi type="italic">You shall not give your daughters unto their sons,</hi> &c., which is taken from <reference osisRef="Deut.7.3">Deut. vii. 3</reference>. When we would reclaim people from sin we must show them the sinfulness of it in the glass of the commandment. (2.) He quotes a precedent, to show the pernicious consequences of it, which made it necessary to be animadverted upon by the government (<reference osisRef="Neh.13.26">v. 26</reference>): <hi type="italic">Did not Solomon king of Israel sin by these things?</hi> The falls of great and good men are recorded in order that we may take warning by them to shun the temptations which they were overcome by. Solomon was famous for wisdom; there was no king like him for it; yet, when he married strange wives, his wisdom could not secure him from their snares, nay, it departed from him, and he did very foolishly. He was beloved of God, but his marrying strange wives threw him out of God's favour, and went near to extinguish the holy fire of grace in his soul: he was king over all Israel; but his doing this occasioned the loss of ten of his twelve tribes. You plead that you can marry strange wives and yet retain the purity of Israelites; but Solomon himself could not; even <hi type="italic">him did outlandish women cause to sin.</hi> Therefore let him that <hi type="italic">thinks he stands take heed lest he fall</hi> when he runs upon such a precipice. <div eID="gen8963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8964" type="x-p"/> 2. He showed himself highly displeased at it, that he might awaken them to a due sense of the evil of it: <hi type="italic">He contended with them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Neh.13.25">v. 25</reference>. They offered to justify themselves in what they did, but he showed them how frivolous their excuses were, and argued it warmly with them. When he had silenced them he <hi type="italic">cursed them,</hi> that is, he denounced the judgments of God against them, and showed them what their sin deserved. He then picked out some of them that were more obstinate than the rest, and fit to be made examples, and <hi type="italic">smote them</hi> (that is, ordered them to be beaten by the proper officers according to the law, <reference osisRef="Deut.25.2-Deut.25.3">Deut. xxv. 2, 3</reference>), to which he added this further mark of infamy that he <hi type="italic">plucked off their hair,</hi> or cut or shaved it off; for it may so be understood. Perhaps they had prided themselves in their hair, and therefore he took it off to deform and humble them, and put them to shame; it was, in effect, to stigmatize them, at least for a time. Ezra, in this case, had plucked off his own hair, in holy sorrow for the sin; Nehemiah plucked off their hair, in a holy indignation at the sinners. See the different tempers of wise, and good, and useful men, and the divers graces, as well as divers gifts, of the same Spirit. <div eID="gen8964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8965" type="x-p"/> 3. He obliged them not to take any more such wives, and separated those whom they had taken: <hi type="italic">He cleansed them from all strangers,</hi> both men and women (<reference osisRef="Neh.13.30">v. 30</reference>), and made them promise with an oath that they would never do so again, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.25">v. 25</reference>. Thus did he try all ways and means to put a stop to this mischief and to prevent another relapse into this disease. <div eID="gen8965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8966" type="x-p"/> 4. He took particular care of the priests' families, that they might not lie under this stain, this guilt. He found, upon enquiry, that a branch of the high priest's own family, one of his grandsons, had married a daughter of Sanballat, that notorious enemy of the Jews (<reference osisRef="Neh.2.10">ch. ii. 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.4.1">iv. 1</reference>), and so had, in effect, twisted interests with the Samaritans, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.28">v. 28</reference>. How little love had that man either to God or his country who could make himself in duty and interest a friend to him that was a sworn enemy to both. It seems this young priest would not put away his wife, and therefore Nehemiah <hi type="italic">chased him from him,</hi> deprived him, degraded him, and made him for ever incapable of the priesthood. Josephus says that this expelled priest was Manasseh, and that when Nehemiah drove him away he went to his father-in-law Sanballat, who built him a temple upon Mount Gerazim, like that at Jerusalem, and promised him he should be high priest in it, and that then was laid the foundation of the Samaritans' pretensions, which continued warm to our Saviour's time. <reference osisRef="John.4.20">John iv. 20</reference>, <hi type="italic">Our fathers worshipped in this mountain.</hi> When Nehemiah had thus expelled one that had forfeited the honour of the priesthood he again posted the <hi type="italic">priests and Levites every one in his business,</hi> <reference osisRef="Neh.13.30">v. 30</reference>. It was no loss to them to part with one that was the scandal of their cloth; the work would be done better without him. When Judas had gone out Christ said, <hi type="italic">Now is the Son of Man glorified,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.13.30-John.13.31">John xiii. 30, 31</reference>. Here are Nehemiah's prayers on this occasion. (1.) He prays, <hi type="italic">Remember them, O my God!</hi> <reference osisRef="Neh.13.29">v. 29</reference>. "Lord, convince and convert them; put them in mind of what they should be and do, that they may come to themselves." Or, "Remember them to reckon with them for their sin; remember it against them." If we take it so, this prayer is a prophecy that God would remember it against them. Those that defile the priesthood despise God, and shall be lightly esteemed. Perhaps they were too many and too great for him to deal with. "Lord" (says he), "deal thou with them; take the work into thy own hands." (2.) He prays, <hi type="italic">Remember me, O my God!</hi> <reference osisRef="Neh.13.31">v. 31</reference>. The best services done to the public have sometimes been forgotten by those for whom they were done (<reference osisRef="Eccl.9.15">Eccl. ix. 15</reference>); therefore Nehemiah refers it to God to recompense him, takes him for his paymaster, and then doubts not but he shall be well paid. This may well be the summary of our petitions; we need no more to make us happy than this: <hi type="italic">Remember me, O my God! for good.</hi>  <chapter eID="Neh.13"/> <div eID="gen8966" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen8715" osisID="Neh" type="book"/>

entries.2f0a7331c048e35f0804d200465754ed41220682: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4390"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 13</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Neh.13.1-Neh.13.9">Ne 13:1-9</reference>. Upon the Reading of the Law Separation Is Made from the Mixed Multitude.</title> <div sID="gen6355" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4390"/><hi type="bold">1. On that day--</hi>This was not immediately consequent on the dedication of the city wall and gates, but after Nehemiah's return from the Persian court to Jerusalem, his absence having extended over a considerable period. The transaction here described probably took place on one of the periodical occasions for the public readings of the law, when the people's attention was particularly directed to some violations of it which called for immediate correction. There is another instance afforded, in addition to those which have already fallen under our notice, of the great advantages resulting from the public and periodical reading of the divine law. It was an established provision for the religious instruction of the people, for diffusing a knowledge and a reverence for the sacred volume, as well as for removing those errors and corruptions which might, in the course of time, have crept in.<div eID="gen6355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6356" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Ammonite and the Moabite should not come into the congregation of God for ever--</hi>that is, not be incorporated into the Israelitish kingdom, nor united in marriage relations with that people (<reference osisRef="Deut.23.3">De 23:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.23.4">4</reference>). This appeal to the authority of the divine law led to a dissolution of all heathen alliances (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.2">Ne 9:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezra.10.3">Ezr 10:3</reference>). <div eID="gen6356" type="x-p"/>
entries.0d8059ab1016aaa096b3697efc86b9eb3e8e1617: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4391"/><div sID="gen6357" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4391"/><hi type="bold">4-5. before this--</hi>The practice of these mixed marriages, in open neglect or violation of the law, had become so common, that even the pontifical house, which ought to have set a better example, was polluted by such an impure mixture.<div eID="gen6357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6358" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Eliashib the priest ... was allied unto Tobiah--</hi>This person was the high priest (<reference osisRef="Neh.13.28">Ne 13:28</reference>; also <reference osisRef="Neh.3.1">Ne 3:1</reference>), who, by virtue of his dignified office, had the superintendence and control of the apartments attached to the temple. The laxity of his principles, as well as of his practice, is sufficiently apparent from his contracting a family connection with so notorious an enemy of Israel as Tobiah. But his obsequious attentions had carried him much farther; for to accommodate so important a person as Tobiah on his occasional visits to Jerusalem, Eliashib had provided him a splendid apartment in the temple. The introduction of so gross an impropriety can be accounted for in no other way than by supposing that in the absence of the priests and the cessation of the services, the temple was regarded as a common public building, which might, in the circumstances, be appropriated as a palatial residence. <div eID="gen6358" type="x-p"/>
entries.a87d62f570b5ba97cb1a6e13258ffbf3088f6d6e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4392"/><div sID="gen6359" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4392"/><hi type="bold">6-9. But in all this was not I at Jerusalem--</hi>Eliashib (concluding that, as Nehemiah had departed from Jerusalem, and, on the expiry of his allotted term of absence, had resigned his government, he had gone not to return) began to use great liberties, and, there being none left whose authority or frown he dreaded, allowed himself to do things most unworthy of his sacred office, and which, though in unison with his own irreligious character, he would not have dared to attempt during the residence of the pious governor. Nehemiah resided twelve years as governor of Jerusalem, and having succeeded in repairing and refortifying the city, he at the end of that period returned to his duties in Shushan. How long [Nehemiah] remained there is not expressly said, but "after certain days," which is a Scripture phraseology for a year or a number of years, he obtained leave to resume the government of Jerusalem; to his deep mortification and regret, he found matters in the neglected and disorderly state here described. Such gross irregularities as were practised, such extraordinary corruptions as had crept in, evidently imply the lapse of a considerable time. Besides, they exhibit the character of Eliashib, the high priest, in a most unfavorable light; for while he ought, by his office, to have preserved the inviolable sanctity of the temple and its furniture, his influence had been directly exercised for evil; especially he had given permission and countenance to a most indecent outrage--the appropriation of the best apartments in the sacred building to a heathen governor, one of the worst and most determined enemies of the people and the worship of God. The very first reform Nehemiah on his second visit resolved upon, was the stopping of this gross profanation [by Eliashib]. The chamber which had been polluted by the residence of the idolatrous Ammonite was, after undergoing the process of ritual purification (<reference osisRef="Num.15.9">Nu 15:9</reference>), restored to its proper use--a storehouse for the sacred vessels. <div eID="gen6359" type="x-p"/>
entries.a1786d093d506fdbf757c58eaaadd5aa87fbc8de: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4393"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Neh.13.10-Neh.13.14">Ne 13:10-14</reference>. Nehemiah Reforms the Officers in the House of God.</title> <div sID="gen6360" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4393"/><hi type="bold">10-13. And I perceived that the portions of the Levites had not been given them--</hi>The people, disgusted with the malversations of Eliashib, or the lax and irregular performance of the sacred rites, withheld the tithes, so that the ministers of religion were compelled for their livelihood to withdraw to their patrimonial possessions in the country. The temple services had ceased; all religious duties had fallen into neglect. The money put into the sacred treasury had been squandered in the entertainment of an Ammonite heathen, an open and contemptuous enemy of God and His people. The return of the governor put an end to these disgraceful and profane proceedings. He administered a sharp rebuke to those priests to whom the management of the temple and its services was committed, for the total neglect of their duties, and the violation of the solemn promises which they had made to him at his departure. He upbraided them with the serious charge of having not only withheld from men their dues, but of having robbed God, by neglecting the care of His house and service. And thus having roused them to a sense of duty and incited them to testify their godly sorrow for their criminal negligence by renewed devotedness to their sacred work, Nehemiah restored the temple services. He recalled the dispersed Levites to the regular discharge of their duties; while the people at large, perceiving that their contributions would be no longer perverted to improper uses, willingly brought in their tithes as formerly. Men of integrity and good report were appointed to act as trustees of the sacred treasures, and thus order, regularity, and active service were re-established in the temple. <div eID="gen6360" type="x-p"/>
entries.0c3e1669fc6d2f9aeb8f9c49f19e098ac567ee25: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4394"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Neh.13.15-Neh.13.31">Ne 13:15-31</reference>. The Violation of the Sabbath.</title> <div sID="gen6361" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4394"/><hi type="bold">15-22. In those days saw I in Judah some treading wine-presses on the sabbath--</hi>The cessation of the temple services had been necessarily followed by a public profanation of the Sabbath, and this had gone so far that labor was carried on in the fields, and fish brought to the markets on the sacred day. Nehemiah took the decisive step of ordering the city gates to be shut, and not to be opened, till the Sabbath was past; and in order to ensure the faithful execution of this order, he stationed some of his own servants as guards, to prevent the introduction of any commodities on that day. On the merchants and various dealers finding admission denied them, they set up booths outside the walls, in hopes of still driving a traffic with the peasantry; but the governor threatened, if they continued, to adopt violent measures for their removal. For this purpose a body of Levites was stationed as sentinels at the gate, with discretionary powers to protect the sanctification of the Sabbath. <div eID="gen6361" type="x-p"/>
entries.6453afefe19bb9e72960b193045d8019d3106242: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4395"/><div sID="gen6362" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4395"/><hi type="bold">24. could not speak in the Jews' language, but according to the language of each people--</hi>a mongrel dialect imbibed from their mothers, together with foreign principles and habits. <div eID="gen6362" type="x-p"/>
entries.c5782d4c432e4af5fb7d871b6ce8d1c447c513f7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4396"/><div sID="gen6363" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4396"/><hi type="bold">25. cursed them--</hi>that is, pronounced on them an anathema which entailed excommunication.<div eID="gen6363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6364" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">smote ... and plucked off their hair--</hi>To cut off the hair of offenders seems to be a punishment rather disgraceful than severe; yet it is supposed that pain was added to disgrace, and that they tore off the hair with violence as if they were plucking a bird alive. <chapter eID="Neh.13"/><div eID="gen6364" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen6225" osisID="Neh" type="book"/>

entries.bb2a0857738b5b5b6c4bf2f00c9b1e8e9f4901d9: <div eID="gen15324" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen15325" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15326" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15326" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15325" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15327" type="x-p"/> The law is read, which commands that the Ammonite and Moabite should be separated from the congregation, on which they separate all the mixed multitude, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.1-Neh.13.3">Neh 13:1-3</reference>. Eliashib the high priest having not only joined opinion with Sanballat, but being also allied to Tobiah the Ammonite, and having given him some of the chambers in the court of the house of God, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.4">Neh 13:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.5">Neh 13:5</reference>; Nehemiah casts out the goods of Tobiah, and purifies the chambers, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.6-Neh.13.9">Neh 13:6-9</reference>. He rectifies several evils; and the people bring the tithes of all things to the treasuries, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.10-Neh.13.12">Neh 13:10-12</reference>. He appoints treasurers, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.13">Neh 13:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.14">Neh 13:14</reference>; finds that the Sabbaths had been greatly profaned by buying and selling, and rectifies this abuse, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.15-Neh.13.22">Neh 13:15-22</reference>; finds Jews that had married strange wives; against whom he testifies, and expels one of the priests who had married the daughter of Sanballat the Horonite, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.23-Neh.13.29">Neh 13:23-29</reference>. He cleanses them from all strangers, makes a final regulation, and prays for God's mercy to himself, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.30">Neh 13:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.31">Neh 13:31</reference>. <div eID="gen15327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15328" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen15328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15329" type="x-p"/> On that day - I am quite of Calmet's mind that the transaction detailed in this chapter did not immediately succeed the dedication of the walls of Jerusalem. It is most likely that, when this dedication was ended, Nehemiah returned to Babylon, as himself particularly marks, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.6">Neh 13:6</reference>, for he did return in the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes; and then, after certain days, supposed to be about the term of one year, he got leave to return to Jerusalem to see how matters were conducted: and there he found the evils which he mentions in this chapter, and which he redressed in the manner himself describes. See the introduction to this book. <div eID="gen15329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15330" type="x-p"/> Should not come into the congregation - That is, Ye shall not form any kind of matrimonial alliance with them. This, and this alone, is the meaning of the law.
entries.61c094b4a400022ad3de88345125322522a7a637: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen15330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15331" type="x-p"/> They separated from Israel all the mixed multitude - They excluded all strange women, and all persons, young and old, who had been born of these illegal connections.
entries.4a3fd2acc342794ef1969bf31241a2efb5768f5b: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen15331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15332" type="x-p"/> Eliashib the priest - Perhaps this was a different person from Eliashib the high priest; but there is no indubitable evidence that he was not the same. If he was high priest, he was very unfaithful to the high charge which he had received; and a reproach to the priesthood. He had married his grandson to Sanballat's daughter: this produced a connection with Tobiah, the fast friend of Sanballat; in whose favor he polluted the house of God, giving him one of the chambers for his ordinary residence, which were appointed for the reception of the tithes, oblations, etc., that came to the house of God.
entries.3d3c4fdb70d3742c084b4ee919d41fc750830143: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen15332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15333" type="x-p"/> Was not I at Jerusalem - Nehemiah came to Jerusalem in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes, and remained there till the thirty-second year, twelve years: then returned to Babylon, and staid one year; got leave to revisit his brethren; and found matters as stated in this chapter.
entries.deadc0afab06c04b638d51cd1813cef9b614863c: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen15333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15334" type="x-p"/> I cast forth all the household stuff of Tobiah - He acted as Jesus Christ did when he found the courts of the Lord's house profaned: He overthrew the tables of the moneychangers, and the seats of those who sold doves.
entries.2c08de8ef3b2f2ffbb977bfad876d01e1e5bbd52: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen15334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15335" type="x-p"/> The portions of the Levites had not been given - Hence we find they were obliged to abandon the sacred service, and betake themselves to cultivate the land for their support. This was the fault of the rulers, who permitted all these abuses.
entries.b10a970c129ad4dc49722e0c32a8a705bd84ea56: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen15335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15336" type="x-p"/> Why is the house of God forsaken? - They had all solemnly promised, <reference osisRef="Neh.10.39">Neh 10:39</reference>, that they would never forsake the house of their God; but, alas, how soon is this forgotten! Nehemiah used their own words here by way of reproof.
entries.f2b3a2bb21fa507a992d2e351117f61d27208873: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen15336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15337" type="x-p"/> They were counted faithful - They were reported to me as persons in whom I could confide; they had been steady in God's ways and work, while others had been careless and relaxed.
entries.a15c94352c7493d19fa5d4d1f4067f9125869b1e: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen15337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15338" type="x-p"/> Wipe not out my good deeds - If thou wert strict to mark what is done amiss, even my good deeds must be wiped out; but, Lord, remember me in thy mercy, and let my upright conduct be acceptable to thee!
entries.6c2a3ffdc3040c6f9d44cfdd543a1f4bf0a3d183: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen15338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15339" type="x-p"/> Treading wine-presses - The Sabbath appears to have been totally disregarded.
entries.2afddd12efcdd4805dc502ad483aa887202a3f0a: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen15339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15340" type="x-p"/> I contended with the nobles - These evils took place through their negligence; and this I proved before them.
entries.c3aad3b248f78c09a492bfa06bb3896c3c169313: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen15340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15341" type="x-p"/> When the gates - began to be dark - After sunset on Friday evening he caused the gates to be shut, and kept them shut all the Sabbath; and, as he could not trust the ordinary officers, he set some of his own servants to watch the gates, that no person might enter for the purpose of traffic.
entries.8cc260518c1d210c3cb380ee44e6cf45957a9b52: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen15341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15342" type="x-p"/> So the merchants - lodged without Jerusalem - They exposed their wares for sale on the outside of the walls.
entries.f5c2ee07062fef7984c1ab20b7c1a4a982e2e727: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen15342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15343" type="x-p"/> I will lay hands on you - I will imprison every man of you. This had the desired effect; they came no more.
entries.5be51f2d4cdb7c8236811f92a5da29ae79b1da74: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen15343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15344" type="x-p"/> Spare me according to the greatness of thy mercy - By some Nehemiah has been thought to deal with God too much on the principle of merit. That he wished God to remember him for good, is sufficiently evident; and who does not wish the same? But that he expected heaven because of his good deeds, does not appear. Indeed, the concluding clause of this verse proves the contrary, and shows that he expected nothing from God but through the greatness of his mercy. Shame on those who, with this evidence before them, brand this good man with the epithet of workmonger! a man who, in inward holiness, outward usefulness, and genuine love to God and man, was worth ten score of such self-called believers.
entries.a7fa053a5de5b8d062279dce0e1d133581e40ab9: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen15344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15345" type="x-p"/> Half in the speech of Ashdod - There were children in the same family by Jewish and Philistine mothers. As the Jewish mother would always speak to her children in Hebrew or Chaldee, so they learnt to speak these languages; and as the Ashdod mother would always speak to her children in the Ashdod language, so they learnt that tongue. Thus there were, in the same family, children who could not understand each other; half, or one part, speaking one language, and the other part another. Children of different wives did not ordinarily mingle together; and the wives had separate apartments. This is a better explanation than that which intimates that the same child spoke a jargon, half Ashdod and half Hebrew.
entries.d0710b786604cf82fa235e3eae4057832ac19d1f: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen15345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15346" type="x-p"/> I contended with them - Proved the fact against these iniquitous fathers, in a legal assembly. <div eID="gen15346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15347" type="x-p"/> And cursed them - Denounced the judgments of God and the sentence of the law upon them. <div eID="gen15347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15348" type="x-p"/> Smote certain of them - Had them punished by whipping. <div eID="gen15348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15349" type="x-p"/> And plucked off their hair - Had them shaven, as a mark of the greatest ignominy. <div eID="gen15349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15350" type="x-p"/> And made them swear by God, saying, Ye shall not give - Caused them to bind themselves by an oath, that they would make no intermarriages with those who were not of the seed of Israel.
entries.4885318a9204038579bb48fd74bf7ab3f8188725: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen15350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15351" type="x-p"/> Did not Solomon - Have you not had an awful example before you? What a heavy curse did Solomon's conduct bring upon himself and upon the people, for a conduct such as yours?
entries.307d845b6bcfb2e43795e6ca93d9a0f6e37b087e: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen15351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15352" type="x-p"/> Shall we then hearken unto you - If God spared not Solomon, who was so much beloved of Him, shall we spare you, who by your conduct are bringing down God's judgments upon Israel?
entries.3c60aa4cb9bbe473ae99e847f6f7e7ead478b1c0: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen15352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15353" type="x-p"/> One of the sons of Joiada - This was Manasseh, brother of Jaddua, son of Joiada, and grandson of Eliashib the high priest. <div eID="gen15353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15354" type="x-p"/> I chased him from me - Struck him off the list of the priests, and deemed him utterly unworthy of all connection and intercourse with truly religious people.
entries.05f2d4ef440c922a3a2b66d0dc45290b45728f89: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen15354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15355" type="x-p"/> Because they have defiled the priesthood - God, therefore, will remember their iniquities against them, and punish them for their transgressions. These words of Nehemiah are to be understood declaratively.
entries.35327015e83c019ac73de474c7f1cbeed2ab1111: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen15355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15356" type="x-p"/> For the wood-offering - This was a most necessary regulation: without it the temple service could not have gone forward; and therefore Nehemiah mentions this as one of the most important services he had rendered to his nation. See <reference osisRef="Neh.10.34">Neh 10:34</reference>. <div eID="gen15356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15357" type="x-p"/> Remember me, O my God, for good - This has precisely the same meaning with, O my God, have mercy upon me! and thus alone it should be understood. <div eID="gen15357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15358" type="x-p"/> Of Nehemiah the Jews speak as one of the greatest men of their nation. His concern for his country, manifested by such unequivocal marks, entitles him to the character of the first patriot that ever lived. In the course of the Divine providence, he was a captive in Babylon; but there his excellences were so apparent, that he was chosen by the Persian king to fill an office the most respectable and the most confidential in the whole court. Here he lived in ease and affluence; he lacked no manner of thing that was good; and here he might have continued to live, in the same affluence and in the same confidence: but he could enjoy neither, so long as his people were distressed, the sepulchres of his fathers trodden under foot, the altars of his God overturned, and his worship either totally neglected or corrupted. He sought the peace of Jerusalem; he prayed to God for it; and was willing to sacrifice wealth, ease, and safety, and even life itself, if he might be the instrument of restoring the desolations of Israel. And God, who saw the desire of his heart, and knew the excellences with which he had endowed him, granted his request, and gave him the high honor of restoring the desolated city of his ancestors, and the pure worship of their God. On this account he has been considered by several as an expressive type of Jesus Christ, and many parallels have been shown in their lives and conduct. <div eID="gen15358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15359" type="x-p"/> I have already, in several notes, vindicated him from all mercenary and interested views, as well as from all false notions of religion, grounded on human merit. For disinterestedness, philanthropy, patriotism, prudence, courage, zeal, humanity, and every virtue that constitutes a great mind, and proves a soul in deep communion with God, Nehemiah will ever stand conspicuous among the greatest men of the Jewish nation, and an exemplar worthy to be copied by the first patriots in every nation under heaven. <div eID="gen15359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15360" type="x-p"/> It has already been observed that, in the Jewish canon, Ezra and Nehemiah make but one book; and that both have been attributed, but without reason, to the same author: hence the Syriac version ends with this colophon - The end of the book of Ezra, the scribe, in which are contained two thousand three hundred and sixty-one verses.  <chapter eID="Neh.13"/> <div eID="gen15360" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen14923" osisID="Neh" type="book"/>

entries.1cb836276aa3823927be9eea332ad8c3f551dd88: <reference osisRef="Neh.13.1-Neh.13.2">Neh 13:1-2</reference> <hi type="italic">Public reading of the law, and separation from strangers</hi>. - Neh 13:1. At a public reading of the law, it was found written therein, that no Ammonite or Moabite should come into the congregation of God, because they met not the children of Israel with bread and with water, but hired Balaam to curse them, though God turned the curse into a blessing. This command, found in <reference osisRef="Deut.23.4-Deut.23.6">Deu 23:4-6</reference>, is given in full as to matter, though slightly abbreviated as to form. The sing. ישׂכּר relates to Balak king of Moab, Num 22:2., and the suffix of עליו to Israel as a nation; see the explanation of Deu 23:4.
entries.ef6fd507649f9ef6fc82d47332ae007870559d07: <reference osisRef="Neh.13.3">Neh 13:3</reference> <div eID="gen6662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6663" type="x-p"/> This law being understood, all strangers were separated from Israel. ערב is taken from <reference osisRef="Exod.12.38">Exo 12:38</reference>, where it denotes the mixed multitude of non-Israelitish people who followed the Israelites at their departure from Egypt. The word is here transferred to strangers of different heathen nationalities living among the Israelites. The date of the occurrence here related cannot be more precisely defined from the ההוּא בּיּום. Public readings of the law frequently took place in those days, as is obvious from Neh 8 and 9, where we learn that in the seventh month the book of the law was publicly read, not only on the first and second days, but also daily during the feast of tabernacles, and again on the day of prayer and fasting on the twenty-fourth of the month. It appears, however, from מזּה לפני, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.4">Neh 13:4</reference>, compared with <reference osisRef="Neh.13.6">Neh 13:6</reference>, that the reading <reference osisRef="Neh.13.1-Neh.13.3">Neh 13:1-3</reference> took place in the interval between Nehemiah’s first and second stay at Jerusalem. This view is not opposed by the facts mentioned Neh 13:4. and 23f. The separation of the ערב could not be carried out at once; and hence, notwithstanding repeated resolutions to sever themselves from strangers (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.2">Neh 9:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.10.31">Neh 10:31</reference>), cases to the contrary might be discovered, and make fresh separations needful.
entries.934fadf8eef9bbd47538bac077072f531fb7a260: <reference osisRef="Neh.13.4-Neh.13.5">Neh 13:4-5</reference> <hi type="italic">Nehemiah, on his return to Jerusalem, reforms the irregularities that had broken out during his absence.</hi> - <reference osisRef="Neh.13.4">Neh 13:4</reference>-9. While Nehemiah was at Babylon with King Artaxerxes, Eliashib the high priest had given up to his relative, Tobiah the Ammonite (<reference osisRef="Neh.2.10">Neh 2:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.4.3">Neh 4:3</reference>, and elsewhere), a large chamber in the temple, i.e., in the fore-court of the temple (v. 7), probably for his use as a dwelling when he visited Jerusalem (see rem. on v. 8). On his return, Nehemiah immediately cast all the furniture of Tobiah out of this chamber, purified the chambers, and restored them to their proper use as a magazine for the temple stores. מזּה לפני, before this (comp. Ewald, §315, <hi type="italic">c</hi>), refers to the beforementioned separation of the ערב from Israel (<reference osisRef="Neh.13.3">Neh 13:3</reference>). Eliashib the priest is probably the high priest of that name (<reference osisRef="Neh.3.1">Neh 3:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.12.10">Neh 12:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.12.22">Neh 12:22</reference>). This may be inferred from the particular: set over (he being set over) the chambers of the house of our God; for such oversight of the chambers of the temple would certainly be entrusted to no simple priest, though this addition shows that this oversight did not absolutely form part of the high priest’s office. For נתן, in the sense of to set, to place over, comp. 1Ki 2:35; the construction with בּ instead of על is, however, unusual, but may be derived from the local signification of בּ, upon, over. Ewald and Bertheau are for reading לשׁכת instead of the sing. לשׁכּת, because in <reference osisRef="Neh.13.5">Neh 13:5</reference> it is not הלּשׁכּה that is spoken of, but a large chamber. לשׁכּת may, however, be also understood collectively. Eliashib, being a relation of Tobiah (קרוב like Rth 2:20), prepared him a chamber. The predicate of the sentence, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.4">Neh 13:4</reference>, follows in <reference osisRef="Neh.13.5">Neh 13:5</reference> with ויּעשׂ, in the form of a conclusion following the accessory sentence of the subject. How Tobiah was related to Eliashib is nowhere stated. Bertheau conjectures that it was perhaps only through the circumstance that Johanan, the son of Tobiah, had married a daughter of Meshullam ben Berechiah (<reference osisRef="Neh.6.18">Neh 6:18</reference>), who, according to <reference osisRef="Neh.3.30">Neh 3:30</reference>, was a priest or Levite, and might have been nearly related to the high priest. “A great chamber,” perhaps made so by throwing several chambers into one, as older expositors have inferred from <reference osisRef="Neh.13.9">Neh 13:9</reference>, according to which Nehemiah, after casting out the goods of Tobiah, had the chambers (plural) cleansed. The statement also in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Neh.13.5">Neh 13:5</reference></hi>, that there (in this great chamber) were aforetime laid up not only the meat-offerings (i.e., oil and flour, the materials for them), the incense, and the sacred vessels, but also the tithe of the corn, the new wine, and the oil, and the heave-offerings of the priests, seems to confirm this view. This tenth is designated as הלויּם מצות, the command of the Levites, i.e., what was apportioned to the Levites according to the law, the legal dues for which משׁפּט is elsewhere usual; comp. <reference osisRef="Deut.18.3">Deu 18:3</reference>; 1Sa 2:13. The heave-offering of the priest is the tenth of their tenth which the Levites had to contribute, Neh 10:39.
entries.c00c811a81f628ca9869c4daf61d1f1879702907: <reference osisRef="Neh.13.6">Neh 13:6</reference> <div eID="gen6663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6664" type="x-p"/> In all this, i.e., while this was taking place, I was not in Jerusalem; for in the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes I went to the king, and after the lapse of some days I entreated the king (נשׁאל like <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.6">1Sa 20:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.28">1Sa 20:28</reference>). What he entreated is not expressly stated; but it is obvious from what follows, ”and I came to Jerusalem,” that it was permission to return to Judea. Even at his first journey to Jerusalem, Nehemiah only requested leave to make a temporary sojourn there, without giving up his post of royal cup-bearer; comp. Neh 2:5. Hence, after his twelve years’ stay in Jerusalem, he was obliged to go to the king and remain some time at court, and then to beg for fresh leave of absence. How long he remained there cannot be determined, - ימים לקץ, after the lapse of days, denoting no definite interval; comp. Gen 4:3. The view of several expositors, that ימים means a year, is devoid of proof. The stay of Nehemiah at court must have lasted longer than a year, since so many illegal acts on the part of the community as Nehemiah on his return discovered to have taken place, could not have occurred in so short a time. Artaxerxes is here called king of Babylon, because the Persian kings had conquered the kingdom of Babylon, and by this conquest obtained dominion over the Jews. Nehemiah uses this title to express also the fact that he had travelled to Babylon.
entries.154d7d0ae2af7f01e5004125a92f123b90b61494: <reference osisRef="Neh.13.7">Neh 13:7</reference> <div eID="gen6664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6665" type="x-p"/> At his return he directed his attention to the evil committed by Eliashib in preparing a chamber in the court of the temple (בּ הבין like Ezr 8:15) for Tobiah.
entries.11a019e5f4b4bed391e86bb6cf28a9040c4b51b0: <reference osisRef="Neh.13.8-Neh.13.9">Neh 13:8-9</reference> <div eID="gen6665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6666" type="x-p"/> This so greatly displeased him, that he cast out all the household stuff of Tobiah, and commanded the chamber to be purified, and the vessels of the house of God, the meat-offering and the frankincense, and probably the tenths and heave-offerings also, the enumeration being here only abbreviated, to be again brought into it. From the words <hi type="italic">household</hi> stuff, it appears that Tobiah used the chamber as a dwelling when he came from time to time to Jerusalem.
entries.0a7cf64f6b8f9f7bdb0577d97531d524a3ff2096: <reference osisRef="Neh.13.10-Neh.13.14">Neh 13:10-14</reference> <div eID="gen6666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6667" type="x-p"/> The payment of dues to the Levites, and the delivery of the tenths and first-fruits, had also been omitted. - Neh 13:10. “And I perceived that the portions of the Levites had not been given; and the Levites and singers who had to do the work, were fled every one to his field.” The Levites, i.e., the assistants of the priests, the singers, and also the porters, who are not expressly mentioned in this passage, were accustomed to receive during the time of their ministry their daily portions of the tenths and first-fruits (<reference osisRef="Neh.12.47">Neh 12:47</reference>). When then these offerings were discontinued, they were obliged to seek their maintenance from the fields of the towns and villages in which they dwelt (Neh 12:28.), and to forsake the service of the house of God. This is the meaning of the בּרח, to flee to the fields.
